title: Why Have You Rejected Us Forever?

verses.text: Why have You rejected us forever, O God? Why does Your anger smolder against the sheep of Your pasture?
Remember Your congregation, which You purchased long ago and redeemed as the tribe of Your inheritance— Mount Zion where You dwell.
Turn Your steps to the everlasting ruins, to everything in the sanctuary the enemy has destroyed.
Your foes have roared within Your meeting place; they have unfurled their banners as signs,
like men wielding axes in a thicket of trees
and smashing all the carvings with hatchets and picks.
They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground; they have defiled the dwelling place of Your Name.
They said in their hearts, "We will crush them completely." They burned down every place where God met us in the land.
There are no signs for us to see. There is no longer any prophet. And none of us knows how long this will last.
How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You? Will the foe revile Your name forever?
Why do You withdraw Your strong right hand? Stretch it out to destroy them!
Yet God is my King from ancient times, working salvation on the earth.
You divided the sea by Your strength; You smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea;
You crushed the heads of Leviathan; You fed him to the creatures of the desert.
You broke open the fountain and the flood; You dried up the ever-flowing rivers.
The day is Yours, and also the night; You established the moon and the sun.
You set all the boundaries of the earth; You made the summer and winter.
Remember how the enemy has mocked You, O LORD, how a foolish people has spurned Your name.
Do not deliver the soul of Your dove to beasts; do not forget the lives of Your afflicted forever.
Consider Your covenant, for haunts of violence fill the dark places of the land.
Do not let the oppressed retreat in shame; may the poor and needy praise Your name.
Rise up, O God; defend Your cause! Remember how the fool mocks You all day long.
Do not disregard the clamor of Your adversaries, the uproar of Your enemies that ascends continually.

context.author: Asaph, one of David’s chief musicians; his family led Temple singing for centuries (Ezra 2:41). Book Three (Psalms 73-89) opens with eleven psalms of Asaph (73-83), several of which mourn the fall of Jerusalem or of the northern kingdom, so many were written or adapted by later members of his guild.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship, in times of national crisis
context.setting: “Why have You rejected us forever, O God? Why does Your anger smolder against the sheep of Your pasture?” (v.1). “Turn Your steps to the everlasting ruins” (v.3). The enemy roared in God’s meeting place, hacked the carved woodwork with axes, and “burned Your sanctuary to the ground” (vv.4-7). “There are no signs for us to see. There is no longer any prophet. And none of us knows how long this will last” (v.9). Then a memory of God’s power: “Yet God is my King from ancient times” (v.12). He split the sea, crushed the heads of Leviathan, made day and night, summer and winter (vv.13-17). “Rise up, O God; defend Your cause!” (v.22).
context.custom: Solomon’s Temple was paneled with carved cedar, overlaid with gold (1 Kings 6:18, 29). Leviathan and the sea dragons were ancient images of chaos that only God controls; here they also picture Egypt, defeated at the sea (Ezekiel 29:3). Conquering armies set up their banners in captured temples (v.4).
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 75 answers with God’s voice: “When I choose a time, I will judge fairly.”
context.timelineBible: The psalm best fits the Babylonian destruction of the Temple in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8-9; Lamentations 2:7). Revelation pictures Satan as “a huge red dragon” (Revelation 12:3), defeated and thrown down (Revelation 12:9). Isaiah promises that God “will slay the dragon of the sea” (Isaiah 27:1).

overview.summary: Mourning the burned sanctuary and the silence of prophets, the psalmist reminds God that He is King from of old, who crushed the sea monsters, and begs Him to rise up.
overview.settingLine: The sanctuary burned to the ground.

archaeology.t: Burned houses such as the House of Ahiel, with ash and arrowheads from the Babylonian attack.
Records Nebuchadnezzar’s capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC.

overview.discussion: “None of us knows how long this will last” (v.9). How do I pray when I cannot see an end to trouble?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (all 150 in the app). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: Asaph (or a later singer of his guild)
overview.audience: God, who seems to have forgotten

timeline.label: God my King from of old
